speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I chair the Inter-Ministry Committee on Scams, or IMCS in short, which was set up in April 2020.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The IMCS brings together Government agencies, such as MHA, SPF, MCI, MAS and MTI, and also works with private sector partners, such as the Association of Banks in Singapore, or ABS, to coordinate efforts to combat all scam types.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These include phishing scams, job scams, loan scams, just to name a few, as well as e-commerce scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: IMCS focuses its efforts to coordinate across agencies to review the scam types and trends, as well as to propose countermeasures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It also enhances enforcement and responses to these scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Thirdly, IMCS strengthens public education and vigilance against scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: My Statement will focus on two aspects of our anti-scam strategy: enforcement and education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The main challenge in enforcement is that the vast majority of scams are perpetrated by syndicates that are based overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such cases are difficult to investigate and prosecute for three reasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, these scammers are typically part of an organised criminal syndicate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They run sophisticated transnational operations which are not easy to detect or dismantle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The syndicates are well-resourced and adept at using technology to cover their tracks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Thirdly, when monies have already been transferred out of Singapore, recovery is very difficult.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF works closely with our overseas counterparts to exchange information and conduct joint operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, in 2021, SPF’s collaboration with law enforcement agencies, such as the Royal Malaysia Police, as well as Hong Kong, led to the takedown of 16 scam syndicates and the arrest of around 230 persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Coming back to the OCBC phishing scams, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and Mr Dennis Tan asked for an update on the ongoing investigations into the OCBC phishing scam.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Many of the scam websites used in the phishing scam were hosted by web hosting companies that are based overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF has commenced investigations into the local IP addresses linked to the scam and the owners of the local money mule accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF is now also working with INTERPOL and foreign law enforcement agencies to investigate the beneficiaries of the funds transferred overseas and the hosts of the scam websites.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As investigations are right now ongoing, we are not able to divulge any more information at this moment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The OCBC phishing scam cases occurred amidst a rise in the number of scams reported in Singapore, which Mr Ang Wei Neng, Dr Tan Wu Meng and Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is more than a fourfold increase from the 5,147 cases of scams reported in 2017, of which only 16 were phishing scam cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Specifically, for phishing scams involving SMSes impersonating banks in Singapore, there were no cases in 2017, but there were 91 in 2018; 57 in 2019; 149 in 2020; before increasing significantly to 1,021 in 2021, in view of the OCBC phishing scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The OCBC phishing scam alone accounted for 790 customers in the two months from December 2021 to January 2022, by far the largest phishing scam involving spoofed SMSes, as mentioned by Minister Lawrence Wong earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The use of a combination of highly-orchestrated tactics, involving spoofed SMSes appearing in the same thread as genuine messages from the bank and links directing victims to a scam website, as well as the large number of customers targeted in the OCBC scam, shows that the threat is now significantly heightened.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim’s query, in 2021, card fraud cases reported by major credit card issuers in Singapore to MAS formed less than 0.1% of total credit card transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MAS and SPF do not track the percentage of funds recovered for these unauthorised credit card transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked if SPF is sufficiently resourced to combat scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Our officers have been trying to cope with increasing workload and expectations, without proportionate increase in manpower.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will need to review this untenable situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Nevertheless, with whatever resources we have, we have reorganised ourselves for greater efficiency and effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, SPF set up the Anti-Scam Centre (ASC) in 2019 as a specialised unit focused on anti-scam interventions and enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 2021, the ASC conducted 26 islandwide anti-scam operations, which resulted in the arrest of around 7,500 money mules and scammers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The ASC also partners private sector stakeholders to disrupt scammers’ operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, it has worked with telecommunications companies to terminate scam-tainted phone lines, and with online marketplaces to remove suspicious online monikers and advertisements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Since 2019, the ASC has frozen around 24,000 bank accounts suspected of being involved in scam activities and recovered about $160 million in scam proceeds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This would include part of the $17 million lost since 2020 to about 1,300 cases of phishing scams involving spoofed SMSes impersonating banks in Singapore, a question which Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF does not track the amount of funds recovered by scam type.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Recovery of monies lost to scams is very difficult.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where we have been able to, it involved close partnerships with financial institutions, in particular, by having a DBS staff co-located with SPF at the ASC to provide swifter and real-time coordination and intervention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Command will also oversee the newly-formed Scam Strike Teams in the seven Land Divisions, which were set up to enable us to take swifter action against scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As Mr Edward Chia and Mr Christopher de Souza suggested, SPF has also leveraged technology and will continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The ASC uses technology to automate manual work processes, such as the generation of electronic production orders to the banks for the freezing of bank accounts that are associated with scams and sending out personalised crime advisories to members of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will allow the Police resources to focus on essential criminal investigations and enforcement work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF also uses technology, such as ScamShield, to crowdsource information on scam calls and SMSes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It provides SPF with information on emerging trends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This enables SPF to react faster to the various scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Another example is SPF and MAS’ ongoing study with banks to explore the use of enhanced fraud surveillance systems based on artificial intelligence to flag suspicious transactions and identify possible fraudulent behaviour in real-time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, I will touch on improving public education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To Ms Foo Mee Har’s question on how consumers can be better protected, the best defence is a discerning public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, the Government has been creating strong public awareness on scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about the challenges in educating Singaporeans on anti-scam precautions and measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A key finding from the 2019 National Prevalence Survey of Scams was that scam victims tend to lack practical knowledge on safe practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While the majority of scam victims had come across anti-scam public campaigns and messages, many of them could not recall specific scam prevention tips.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They also exhibited poor online hygiene, such as opening emails from unknown sources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Government’s anti-scam public education campaign, called "Spot the Signs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Stop the Crimes", aims to address these challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The campaign emphasises the importance of individual responsibility and also uses real-life examples to build awareness and vigilance on the tell-tale signs of scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As part of this campaign, we have disseminated materials advising the public on scam prevention tips, such as never to share one-time-passwords (OTPs) with unverified parties and to be wary of requests for gift cards and online credits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Mr Mohd Fahmi Bin Aliman asked if there is an age group that is most vulnerable to phishing scams and the common scams that different segments of the population fall prey to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Scam victims are of a wide range of ages; everyone is susceptible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: That said, different profiles of victim falls prey to different types of scam.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, the Government has also rolled out prevention initiatives targeted at specific population segments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF and NCPC have partnered ABS on various initiatives to educate bank customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the banks have introduced an online quiz on scam prevention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They have also sent out advisories to customers to remind them not to share their OTP with others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Banks have also stepped up their efforts to also train their frontline staff to help customers spot signs of scam.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, in June 2021, OCBC staff helped to prevent a 57-year-old customer from being scammed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The customer had wanted to remit around 6,000 euros to her Internet “boyfriend” based in the United States.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: OCBC branch staff noticed that the fund transfer was to be made to a personal bank account in Thailand and suspected that the customer was being scammed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The OCBC staff spent hours trying to dissuade the customer from transferring the funds and worked with SPF officers to try to advise the customer from sending any money.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Eventually and thankfully, they managed to convince the customer that she was being scammed, after the “boyfriend” was not available for a video call that bank staff worked with the customer to arrange.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Another example of a preventative initiative is the “SG Cyber Safe Seniors Programme” launched in June 2021 by the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and SPF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The programme seeks to raise seniors’ awareness of online scams and encourage them to adopt good cyber hygiene.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under the programme, CSA and its partners, such as the SG Digital Office, offer scam prevention tips, including how to spot signs of phishing and avoiding the sharing of personal information and OTPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The IMCS will step up our public education efforts by scaling up targeted outreach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will partner agencies and stakeholders that serve as key touchpoints for population segments of interest and leverage their communications channels to push out anti-scam messages targeted at different segments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, IMCS has started working closely with the Agency for Integrated Care, MOE, MOM and MoneySense to push out anti-scam information and awareness programmes for our seniors, students, even migrant workers and professionals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The IMCS has also started to work with stakeholders from the private sector: partnering ABS to reach out to consumers who use banking services and major e-commerce platforms and marketplaces to reach out to consumers transacting on those online platforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Everyone should also download ScamShield, to filter out scam messages and block scam calls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We are unable to provide Mr Gerald Giam with the percentage of scam calls and SMSes successfully blocked, as ScamShield does not track the number of calls and SMSes made or received by the users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: ScamShield picked up and filtered about 2,000 scam messages used in the OCBC phishing scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Unfortunately, a lot more scam messages managed to reach the SMS inboxes of ScamShield users, mainly because they appeared in the same thread as legitimate messages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This gap will be addressed as agencies enhance our SMS ecosystem, as Minister Josephine Teo explained.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: That said, ScamShield, in itself, is not a panacea and all parts of the ecosystem need to work together to combat scams, including vigilance from all members of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When ScamShield was developed, we made it available to iOS devices first as it was functionally easier to build.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We had, initially, planned to launch the Android version of ScamShield in late 2021, but it was delayed as GovTech had to reprioritise resources towards supporting our efforts against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: IMCS will continue our efforts to encourage the public to download ScamShield, including through community engagements by SPF and Volunteer Crime Prevention Ambassadors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I would also like to call on Members of this House to encourage your residents to download ScamShield.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In concluding, combating scams needs a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Even as SPF steps up enforcement, members of the community still play a vital role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We urge the members of public to be individually alert and also to raise collective awareness by sharing scam prevention tips with your friends and family.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Together, I am confident we can build a safer Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My first question is, will this proposed equitable sharing look at the difference between an unforced error compared to a forced error, where a customer was led or pressured into making an error, as appears to have been the case with the OCBC phishing scam?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The second question, Mr Speaker, will this proposed framework for equitable sharing of losses also consider the speed of the bank response when a consumer is trying to get help?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of my Clementi residents described it thus.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He said, "Imagine you got tricked, someone copied your house keys, they are looting your house now, you call for help and you are put on hold.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You wait to press a number or get to the right department." That is what my resident said and they are worried what happens if this is their experience in a scam.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to be ready for the next character of scams.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, is there a role for white hat scammers, just like there are white hat hackers – white hat scammers actively testing the bank's procedures to look for vulnerabilities before fellow Singaporeans suffer avoidable losses?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, we cannot be fighting the last war, we have to look ahead, anticipate vulnerabilities and continually look at different ways to improve our system, and MAS is certainly committed to this process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not want to get ahead of the process, but I would just want to set out some key principles which the Council is using to guide its deliberations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it should not matter which bank you go to; it has to be applied consistently across the entire industry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, Dr Tan Wu Meng talked of some scenarios about speed and whether or not it is a forced or unforced error.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that is a fair and equitable principle, But, obviously, there are many details to be worked out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the Payments Council chaired by MAS will go about these deliberations with the different stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And I should add, the stakeholders, as I have mentioned earlier, also include players operating the communications infrastructure because we want to ensure that there is proper accountability across the entire ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I agree with the Minister that we need to adopt an ecosystem approach to tackle banking scams.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, given the unprecedented wave of online banking frauds hitting consumers – actually, not just in Singapore, we have read about such accounts in the UK and around the world – may I ask how does MAS fare in terms of anti-scam controls, compared to some of the best practices in other jurisdictions to protect the interests of our consumers?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I want to ask, specifically, whether MAS will be imposing a set of minimum standards for the banks' fraud surveillance system to better protect consumers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS' approach and what MAS has done so far has, in fact, gone beyond the usual practices among financial regulators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In major jurisdictions, regulators do not themselves prescribe the specific anti-scam controls for the banks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, they take a supervisory approach, which means they set up the broad supervisory expectations of the banks, then they place the responsibility on the banks to develop the specific anti-scam measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, the regulators will assess the adequacy of these measures and they will impose penalties if the banks fall short of expectations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is the approach that other regulators take, most regulators will take, and that is also the basic approach that MAS has undertaken.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, as I mentioned, MAS has, in fact, gone beyond most regulators in being quite clear about its expectations, as well as the specific anti-scam measures that are required.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let me assure Members that MAS takes this work very seriously.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It has been, and will continue to do everything it can, working together with other partners and stakeholders to strengthen the security across our digital banking channels and also across the entire digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second question on the framework for the sharing of losses, I do not want to get into details because, as I have highlighted, this is still work in progress.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, as I mentioned just now, our intention is to clearly set out basic responsibilities expected of financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this is work in progress and we will put out the details in due course when we are ready.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For the Minister for Communications and Information, once the sender ID registry becomes a whitelist like what she described just now, will scammers still be able to send SMSes from overseas with the sender ID that is not registered in Singapore's registry?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if so, how would such scam messages be prevented?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For the Minister for Finance, recent scams have demonstrated that SMS is an insecure channel for sending either one-time passwords or hyperlinks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to MAS' Technology Risk Assessment Guidelines to financial institutions, end-to-end encryption should be implemented for the transmission of customers' passwords.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, why is MAS not immediately prohibiting the use of SMS one-time passwords, especially to protect the less tech-savvy customers who are at risk of getting scammed?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Basically, the SMS service providers will be approached by a party to say that here is a message that I would like to send to these numbers in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The imposition that we are making on the SMS Service provider is to look at the header that is being requested by the customer to send it under and check against the registry.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, if a name already appears on the registry, then, regardless of who the customer is or where they are requesting this service from, as long as the name appears in the registry and this party's details do not match the other record in the registry in terms of their UEN, in terms of the path that they described, how they want to send the SMS across, then this business has to be turned away by the SMS service providers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the purpose of having the registry is to allow the SMS service providers to know whether this is a legitimate request and if these signs of legitimate requests are not matched, the requirement for the SMS service provider is to turn away the business.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I hope that that provides an answer to the Member's question.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should highlight that, really, as I mentioned in my speech, there is no single measure that can guarantee the security of digital banking.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is a broader issue that we have to look at holistically and, as I mentioned, we are determined and committed to this process to review the entire ecosystem and strengthen it.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   With the sharp increase in online fraud cases amidst the COVID-19 pandemic which has led to most institutions to minimise in-person transactions, will the Singapore Police Force step up collaboration and education efforts with SG Digital Office and the Silver Generation Office to reach out to and assist seniors, such as increasing its presence in the heartlands by setting up more SG Digital Community Hubs and sending out more Silver Generation Ambassadors to visit seniors at home?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many grandmas and grandpas are unable to understand how ScamShield works.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I will reply in English and I will say a few remarks in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Actually, Minister Josephine Teo has highlighted many of the measures that we have implemented in relation to helping our seniors go digital as well as to continue on our digital transformation journey.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I think the question is a valid one in relation to how this incident may have affected some confidence, especially among our users and seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I want to emphasise that, as I had mentioned in my speech earlier on, the groups of people who are affected by scams are not just the seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In fact, our data showed that the younger people who have been transacting more online are more susceptible, or just as susceptible, to scams.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, there are two areas that we need to focus on in relation to the Member's question.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: One is how can we bolster confidence among our users?

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: That is something that Minister Lawrence Wong, Minister Josephine Teo and I have been trying to explain and let Members know the measures that we are taking to make the digital space a safer environment for all of us to operate in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The second area is to build a more resilient community in the use of the digital space.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: That is something that we have been working with the different stakeholders and partners – Government as well as the private sector – to strengthen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: More specific to Member Don Wee's question on the seniors' programme, we have introduced a number of programmes and, given this incident, we will continue to step up our outreach to our seniors to not just help them to acquire the skillsets but also to explain to them what are the telltale signs of scams and how to protect themselves from scams.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, we will continue to step up these efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I want to end off by saying that this education effort is an important one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We also want to build a Scam Smart Nation, where our people understand the telltale signs and to protect themselves and help one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Singapore has seen a rising number of scam cases in recent years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Therefore, MHA and other Ministries will do our best to work with community partners to strengthen prevention measures and raise awareness against scams.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In 2021, online phishing scams were on the rise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Scammers used various ways to mislead victims into revealing their personal information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Here, I urge everyone to stay alert and not to believe strangers easily, nor to share your personal information or even transfer money.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The public can also download ScamShield from Apple Store.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Don Wee said our grandmas and grandpas might not understand ScamShield.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: However, I believe that once they realise the benefits of ScamShield which offers them greater protection, they will be able to use digital platforms more confidently.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second supplementary question: in working out the shared responsibility between banks and their customers, would MAS consider putting the onus more on the banks on the basis that: one, the banks are more tech-savvy and scam-savvy than the average bank customer and they have better resources to keep up-to-date with the latest tactics; two, it provides additional incentives on the banks to adopt a pre-emptive approach, for example, to consider the scam potential before pushing out new procedures or facilities; and thirdly, it is probably more cost-effective to focus on scam prevention efforts from the ends of a few banks rather than public education on a whole wide range of bank customers?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I can appreciate that there is a lot of interest in this and, as I have said, it is a work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But to quickly answer Ms Poa's two questions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are very mindful that individuals have a different set of resources and capabilities, compared to financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in developing the specific responsibilities for individuals and financial institutions, we will certainly take that into consideration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have one clarification for the Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the issues with scams is that the perpetrators are normally based abroad.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: At the same time, I also mentioned some of the difficulties, including how we can get our foreign law enforcement agency partners to work within their jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: And once the money has been transferred, there are also some difficulties as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: But it is an effort we will continue to do, as we have done in recent times, and we will step up this collaboration with the partners – foreign law enforcement agencies – to try and strengthen our enforcement as well as recovery of lost monies with the foreign banks as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if the Ministry has plans to introduce complementary legislation to bolster the additional regulatory actions that he has already proposed and the reasons are, because while regulation is often useful for guiding actions, to use the example Minister Lawrence Wong raised earlier about allowing certain transactions to be disputed, without the force of law, it might still fail to adequately ensure an equal distribution of liability even in the presence of, as he described, the fair, equitable framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Using the same example, if I may, requiring charges above $50 to be subject to dispute under the Fair Credit Billing Act in the US has meant that financial institutions have, actually, been a lot more proactive in deploying fraud detection systems and securing fraud insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is something that Member Hazel Poa has mentioned as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question is for Minister Josephine Teo and it is to ask if there are plans to comprehensively audit the compliance of technology systems with their official safeguards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I say this because, in a recent little experiment with my Sengkang colleague, Louis Chua, we tried to test the limits of the PayNow system, as applied by banks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The stated PayNow transfer limit, in the absence of additional authentication via token, is meant to be $1,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, we were able to transfer sums in excess of this amount just by instantaneously changing the daily transfer limits, and, again, without any two-factor authentication beyond the PIN prior to executing the transfer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Others have reported similar lapses in banks' checks and balances in guaranteeing customer security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One banking customer, writing to The Straits Times, shared that they were able to breach the credit limit by 1.8 times in transactions occurring over multiple countries in foreign currencies without the incident being flagged.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if new legislation is necessary or amendments to the laws are necessary, we will certainly not rule out those options.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One is in terms of the banks' information systems, IT systems, we classify them as part of our critical information infrastructure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a result of this classification, they are subject to higher requirements and also regular audits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, earlier on, when I had explained, and Minister Lawrence Wong had also explained why this was not a cyber attack or cybersecurity breach, that has to do with the kind of defences that are part of the banking system being a critical information infrastructure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Otherwise, we would not know whether the cyber defences that are intended to be put up are, in fact, effectively done.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I would always caution that this is not something you brag about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Just because the system is sound at any point in time does not mean it is not continuously being subject to testing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And whether it is banks, whether it is our telcos, as part of the operators of our critical information infrastructure, they always also have to conduct their own penetration testing, in order to assure themselves that there are no vulnerabilities or gaps that are glaring and that have not been patched.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second part of it, and his experiment with Mr Louis Chua using PayNow, I think it is very similar to what Dr Tan Wu Meng had already suggested earlier, whether you would consider subjecting your own banking processes to white hat scammers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I think Minister Lawrence Wong had already responded to that question to say that the answer is yes; it is a good suggestion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And we should be seriously thinking about how to do so.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We understand from Minister of State Desmond Tan that once the money is transferred out of Singapore during an Internet scam, it is almost as good as gone.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister for Finance what the proportion of Internet transfers is involving accounts overseas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Is it possible for the local user to opt, by default, to not allow the transfer of money out to overseas, unless authorised otherwise with the two-step verification?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is similar to what local mobile phone users do, where they can disable the auto-roaming so as to minimise the cost.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will continue to look at how these sorts of measures and safeguards can be strengthened.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My residents who came to me to seek help on the recent OCBC bank scam incident shared that information from the bank during the investigation process and the support during the processes itself, were found wanting.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of them had interactions only with the call centre staff and this has left them very afraid and stressed and, indeed, worried that their life savings were kept in limbo.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I explained in my speech just now, we have assessed that OCBC itself, in this incident, could have done better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But with regard to standards, expectations and responsibilities, these are in place today for all the retail banks and we will continue to review and ensure that these standards are set in such a way that provide assurances to customers and hold the banks accountable to meeting these high standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is sobering to learn that our current anti-scam systems are blocking millions of scam calls each month.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If not, are there any plans by the Ministry to safeguard these channels?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I will have to get back to him properly.
